_meta.method: WebSearch result summaries only; WebFetch was blocked by the egress proxy for Wikipedia and most other domains, so facts come from search summaries of the cited pages. Items marked with a 'note' field have conflicting or partial sourcing.

timeline.title: The name 'Parnassus' appears
timeline.text: The name 'Parnassus' was used as early as 1769 for a 300-acre tract of land that later became the Parnassus section of New Kensington.

timeline.title: Fort Crawford built
timeline.text: Continental Army troops built Fort Crawford, a stockade near the mouth of Pucketa Creek, named for Col. William Crawford. Settlers used it as a refuge during attacks and as a storehouse for munitions and supplies.

timeline.title: Fort Crawford abandoned
timeline.text: Fort Crawford was used more or less regularly for about sixteen years and stopped operating in 1793.

timeline.title: Burrell Township formed
timeline.text: Burrell Township was carved out of Allegheny Township by court order and named for Judge Jeremiah Murry Burrell of the Westmoreland County Court.

timeline.title: Major Andrew Arnold settles the Arnold area
timeline.text: The area around Arnold was first settled by Indian fighter Major Andrew Arnold, who gave the city its name. (Wikipedia also gives 1781 as a settlement date.)
timeline.note: Sources differ: 1852 (settlement by Maj. Andrew Arnold) vs. 1781 (settled) in the Wikipedia summary.

timeline.title: Arnold Station opens
timeline.text: Arnold Station, a railroad stop, was established on land given by the Arnold family.

timeline.title: Parnassus becomes a borough
timeline.text: The borough of Parnassus was incorporated. It stayed independent until New Kensington absorbed it decades later.

timeline.title: Lower and Upper Burrell split
timeline.text: Burrell Township was divided into two townships, Lower Burrell and Upper Burrell.

timeline.title: Pittsburgh Reduction Company starts in Pittsburgh
timeline.text: The Pittsburgh Reduction Company, later Alcoa, built its first plant on Smallman Street in Pittsburgh. By 1890 it made 5,000 pounds of aluminum a month.

timeline.title: 'Kensington' planned
timeline.text: The Burrell Improvement Company picked the level riverfront land south of Lower Burrell for a new city and named it 'Kensington'. The name was later changed to 'New Kensington' to avoid postal confusion with the Philadelphia neighborhood.

timeline.title: Great land sale: June 10, 1891
timeline.text: The Burrell Improvement Company held a public lot sale on June 10, 1891, offering free train rides from Pittsburgh. About 500 lots sold for $135,000 in the first three days.

timeline.title: Aluminum works come to New Kensington
timeline.text: Charles M. Hall's Pittsburgh Reduction Company moved its plant 17 miles up the Allegheny River to New Kensington. It was the company's first major aluminum plant outside Pittsburgh.

timeline.title: Chambers Glass Company opens in Arnold
timeline.text: The Chambers Glass Company opened in Arnold and became one of the largest window-glass factories in the United States.

timeline.title: Twelve companies by year's end
timeline.text: By the end of 1891, New Kensington had 12 companies employing 4,000 people.

timeline.title: Borough incorporated
timeline.text: New Kensington was incorporated as a borough on November 26, 1892.

timeline.title: First Jewish merchant
timeline.text: Isaac Claster, a peddler who bought a lot at the 1891 sale, built a clothing store on Tenth Street.

timeline.title: Arnold becomes a borough
timeline.text: Arnold was incorporated as a borough.

timeline.title: Wear-Ever cookware founded
timeline.text: Charles M. Hall and Alfred E. Hunt founded the Aluminum Cooking Utensil Company in New Kensington on October 24, 1901. It sold the Wear-Ever brand, and its top line was called 'Kensington Ware'.

timeline.title: Valley Daily News begins
timeline.text: The Valley Daily News, based in Tarentum, began publishing on June 27, 1904. It is a forerunner of the Valley News Dispatch.

timeline.title: Beth Jacob Congregation incorporated
timeline.text: By 1905 about 25 Jewish families had opened a small synagogue in the 1100 block of Third Avenue. They incorporated Beth Jacob Congregation in May 1907.

timeline.title: Trinity Hospital chartered
timeline.text: Trinity Hospital, later Citizens General Hospital, was chartered on December 12, 1912, at 427 Sixth Ave. in Parnassus.

timeline.title: Alcoa works expand into Arnold
timeline.text: Alcoa's New Kensington Works expanded across the city line into Arnold.

timeline.title: Alcoa donates hospital site
timeline.text: Alcoa donated land at Fourth Avenue and Seventh Street in New Kensington for Citizens General Hospital.

timeline.title: Liberty Theatre opens
timeline.text: The Liberty Theatre opened on May 2, 1921, at Fifth Avenue and Eighth Street.

timeline.title: New Kensington Bridge opens
timeline.text: The C. L. Schmitt Bridge (New Kensington Bridge) over the Allegheny River opened on June 29, 1927.

timeline.title: Alcoa Research Laboratory
timeline.text: Alcoa built its research laboratory on Freeport Road in 1928-1930. Architect Henry Hornbostel designed it as a showcase of aluminum details.

timeline.title: Population 16,762
timeline.text: The census counted 16,762 residents in New Kensington.

timeline.title: Parnassus absorbed
timeline.text: New Kensington absorbed the neighboring borough of Parnassus.
timeline.note: Britannica and TribLIVE say 1931; the Wikipedia summary says 1939.

timeline.title: New Kensington becomes a city
timeline.text: New Kensington was incorporated as a third-class city.

timeline.title: St. Patrick's Day Flood
timeline.text: The March 1936 flood hit the whole Pittsburgh region. In Parnassus, residents were rescued from the second floors of their houses in rowboats.

timeline.title: Arnold becomes a city
timeline.text: Arnold was incorporated as a third-class city.

timeline.title: Population 24,055
timeline.text: New Kensington's population rose to 24,055 in the 1940 census.

timeline.title: Mount St. Peter Church built
timeline.text: Mount St. Peter Church was built at 100 Freeport Road in Art Deco and International styles to a design by Enos Cooke. The Dattola Theatre also opened downtown in 1942.

timeline.title: Population peak: 25,146
timeline.text: New Kensington reached its peak census population of 25,146.

timeline.title: Tarentum Bridge opens
timeline.text: The Tarentum-Valley Heights Bridge opened on February 26, 1952, at a cost of $4.5 million. It charged a ten-cent toll until 1961.

timeline.title: Willie Thrower makes NFL history
timeline.text: New Kensington native Willie Thrower became the first Black quarterback in the NFL's modern era on October 18, 1953, playing for the Chicago Bears.

timeline.title: Penn State New Kensington founded
timeline.text: Penn State's New Kensington Center opened in the First Ward School Building downtown. It moved to the former Parnassus Junior High in 1963 and to its Upper Burrell campus in 1966.

timeline.title: Lower Burrell becomes a city
timeline.text: Lower Burrell was incorporated as a third-class city on January 12, 1959.

timeline.title: New Kensington-Arnold School District formed
timeline.text: The New Kensington-Arnold School District was formed on July 1, 1965. Also by 1965, Alcoa had opened its Alcoa Technical Center in Upper Burrell, having outgrown the Freeport Road lab.

timeline.title: Wear-Ever headquarters leaves
timeline.text: The Aluminum Cooking Utensil Company, later Wear-Ever, moved its headquarters from New Kensington, its home since 1901, to Chillicothe, Ohio.

timeline.title: Alcoa New Kensington Works closes
timeline.text: Alcoa closed its New Kensington Works, which had once employed nearly a quarter of the city. The Schreiber family bought the 66-acre site that year and marketed it as Schreiber Industrial Park.

timeline.title: Valley News Dispatch name
timeline.text: On November 1, 1971, the merged Daily Dispatch and Valley Daily News became the Valley News Dispatch.

timeline.title: Tarentum Bridge renamed
timeline.text: The state Senate renamed the Tarentum Bridge the George D. Stuart Bridge. Siemens also signed the first lease at Schreiber Industrial Park that year.

timeline.title: Two National Register districts
timeline.text: The New Kensington Downtown Historic District (143 contributing buildings) and the New Kensington Production Works Historic District (the Alcoa works, listed May 7, 1998) were added to the National Register of Historic Places.

timeline.title: Citizens General Hospital closes
timeline.text: Citizens General merged with Allegheny Valley Hospital in Harrison under West Penn Allegheny, and the New Kensington hospital closed. Its building was leased as an outpatient center.

timeline.title: Willie Thrower statue
timeline.text: A statue of Willie Thrower was unveiled at Valley High School's Memorial Stadium.

timeline.title: WCCC New Kensington center opens
timeline.text: Westmoreland County Community College opened its New Kensington center at 1150 Fifth Ave. in January 2009.

timeline.title: Tom Guzzo becomes mayor
timeline.text: Tom Guzzo resigned his city council seat to become mayor of New Kensington. He was still mayor in 2026.

timeline.title: AK Research Park
timeline.text: Steve Kubrick's Kubrick Enterprises bought the 17-acre former Alcoa research campus on Freeport Road and renamed it AK Research Park.

timeline.title: Knead Community Cafe opens
timeline.text: Knead Community Cafe, the first pay-what-you-can cafe in Western Pennsylvania, held its grand opening on February 25, 2017, at 1011 Barnes St.

timeline.title: City redevelopment authority buys industrial park
timeline.text: The Redevelopment Authority of the City of New Kensington bought the former Alcoa works (Schreiber Industrial Park).

timeline.title: Corridor of Innovation and Voodoo Brewing
timeline.text: The city launched its Fifth Avenue 'Corridor of Innovation', backed by a Penn State seed grant. Voodoo Brewing opened in the former Ritz Theater at 956 Fifth Ave. on August 21, 2020.

timeline.title: Population 12,170
timeline.text: The 2020 census counted 12,170 New Kensington residents, 4,772 in Arnold and 11,758 in Lower Burrell.

timeline.title: Fridays on Fifth and St. Patrick's parade begin
timeline.text: The monthly Fridays on Fifth food-truck night started downtown in 2021. Lower Burrell's St. Patrick's Day parade was started during the COVID-19 lockdown.

timeline.title: Digital Foundry opens
timeline.text: The Digital Foundry at New Kensington, a 15,044-square-foot smart-manufacturing lab on Fifth Avenue, held its grand opening on June 1, 2022.

timeline.title: Re:Build and the Advanced Manufacturing Park
timeline.text: In May 2023, Re:Build Manufacturing announced an $81 million project at the New Kensington Advanced Manufacturing Park that it said would create 300 jobs. In October, a WCIDC-RIDC joint venture completed its purchase of the park.

timeline.title: New Kensington Bridge rehab
timeline.text: The C. L. Schmitt Bridge closed on July 24, 2023, for a $24.59 million preservation project and reopened on September 1, ahead of Labor Day.

timeline.title: Re:Build begins production
timeline.text: Re:Build finished upgrades to a 175,000-square-foot facility in the park, which straddles the New Kensington-Arnold line, and began manufacturing in early 2025.

timeline.title: Penn State votes to close PSNK
timeline.text: In May 2025, Penn State trustees voted 25-8 to close seven Commonwealth Campuses, including New Kensington, after the spring 2027 semester. The campuses would admit no new students after fall 2025.

timeline.title: Planning the campus's future
timeline.text: The Economic Growth Connection of Westmoreland ran a public visioning survey, 'PSU (Re)New Kensington Campus', on reusing the Upper Burrell campus. No buyer or decision had been announced.

timeline.title: Vacant hospital standoff and data-center questions
timeline.text: The city struggled to reach the California owner of the vacant former Citizens General Hospital. Separately, Mayor Guzzo told residents the city was not in talks with any data-center developers.

neighborhoods.name: Parnassus
neighborhoods.text: The oldest part of town. The name dates to a 1769 land tract, and Fort Crawford (1777) stood at the mouth of Pucketa Creek here. It was an independent borough from 1872 until New Kensington absorbed it (1931 per Britannica; some sources say 1939). Trinity/Citizens General Hospital began here in 1912, and residents were rescued by rowboat in the 1936 flood.

neighborhoods.name: Downtown / Fifth Avenue
neighborhoods.text: The 1891 street grid of avenues running parallel to the river and numbered cross streets. It is a National Register historic district of 143 buildings (1891-1947) and now the five-block 'Corridor of Innovation', home to the Digital Foundry, Corner LaunchBox, WCCC, Voodoo Brewing and Fridays on Fifth.

neighborhoods.name: Valley Heights
neighborhoods.text: A New Kensington neighborhood. The Tarentum Bridge opened in 1952 as the 'Tarentum-Valley Heights Bridge'.

neighborhoods.name: Mount Vernon
neighborhoods.text: A quiet residential neighborhood in the southeast of New Kensington with about 497 residents. Most homes were built between 1940 and 1969.

neighborhoods.name: Valley Camp
neighborhoods.text: Listed as a New Kensington neighborhood.

neighborhoods.name: Pine Manor
neighborhoods.text: Listed as a New Kensington neighborhood, along with Parnassus, Mount Vernon, Valley Camp, Valley Heights and '40 Acres'.

neighborhoods.name: 40 Acres
neighborhoods.text: Listed as a New Kensington neighborhood.

neighborhoods.name: Arnold
neighborhoods.text: A separate third-class city (borough 1896, city 1939) upriver from New Kensington, named for Major Andrew Arnold. It grew around the Chambers Glass Company (1891) and the 1913 Alcoa expansion. It shares the New Kensington-Arnold School District and the Advanced Manufacturing Park with New Kensington. 2020 population: 4,772.

neighborhoods.name: Lower Burrell
neighborhoods.text: A third-class city since January 12, 1959, split from Burrell Township in 1879. It covers 11.52 square miles and had 11,758 residents in 2020. Informal neighborhoods: Bon Air, Braeburn, Braeburn Heights, Central City, Edgecliff, Gladeview, Indian Fields I & II and Kinloch. Its business district overlaps Bon Air, Central City and Gladeview.

facts.name_origin: Named 'Kensington' after Kensington, London. 'New' was added for postal reasons, to avoid confusion with the Kensington neighborhood of Philadelphia.
facts.population_note: Figures for 1900-1920 and 1970-1990 could not be retrieved; Wikipedia's census table was not reachable.

landmarks.name: New Kensington Downtown Historic District
landmarks.text: National Register district (1998) of 143 contributing buildings from about 1891-1947. Highlights include the Mellon Bank Building (1900), PNC Bank (1914), the Wear Ever Building (1914-15), the U.S. Post Office (1933), the Ritz (1921-22), the Datola (1942) and Columbus (1927) theaters, and a White Castle restaurant (c. 1921-28).

landmarks.name: New Kensington Production Works Historic District (Alcoa works)
landmarks.text: A 60-acre National Register district (May 7, 1998) with 35 industrial buildings from about 1899-1947. It includes Alcoa's original plant, which operated from 1891 to 1971, and is documented as HAER PA-337.
landmarks.address: Along the Allegheny River, Seventh/Ninth Street to Sixteenth Street (New Kensington-Arnold)

landmarks.name: New Kensington Advanced Manufacturing Park
landmarks.text: The former Alcoa works and later Schreiber Industrial Park, straddling the New Kensington-Arnold line. It has been owned by a WCIDC-RIDC joint venture since 2023, and Re:Build Manufacturing operates there.

landmarks.name: Alcoa Research Laboratory / AK Research Park
landmarks.text: Henry Hornbostel's limestone laboratory (1928-30), decorated with aluminum doors and fittings and documented as HAER PA-295. It has been redeveloped as AK Research Park since 2011.

landmarks.name: Mount St. Peter Church
landmarks.text: An Art Deco and International-style Catholic church (1942, architect Enos Cooke). Its ceiling is gold tile modeled on Santa Maria Maggiore, and its altar is modeled on St. Peter's Basilica. The parish hosts the yearly Festa Italiana.

landmarks.name: Memorial Park
landmarks.text: A city park of at least 25 acres with veterans' monuments, including the original World War I memorial, an M5 anti-tank gun and an F-80 jet fighter.

landmarks.name: Willie Thrower statue and historical marker
landmarks.text: A statue (2006) at Valley High School's Memorial Stadium and a state historical marker (2003) honoring the NFL's first modern-era Black quarterback.
landmarks.address: Valley Junior/Senior High School, New Kensington

landmarks.name: Digital Foundry at New Kensington
landmarks.text: A 15,044-square-foot smart-manufacturing training and innovation center that opened in 2022. The orange building's sawtooth roof recalls the city's industrial heritage.

landmarks.name: Ritz Theater / Voodoo at the Ritz
landmarks.text: A historic 1920s theater in the downtown historic district, reopened in 2020 as Voodoo Brewing's brewpub.

landmarks.name: Liberty Theater
landmarks.text: A movie theater that opened May 2, 1921. It is documented by HABS/HAER in the Library of Congress.

landmarks.name: Dattola Theatre (later Kensington Theatre)
landmarks.text: Opened in 1942 as the New Dattola Theatre, and briefly reopened as the Kensington Theatre showing classic double features.

landmarks.name: Former Citizens General Hospital
landmarks.text: A 5.5-acre hospital complex on land Alcoa donated in 1915. The hospital closed in 2000, and the building was vacant in 2026 amid a dispute with its out-of-state owner.
landmarks.address: Fourth Avenue and Seventh Street, New Kensington

landmarks.name: Chambers Window Glass Company site
landmarks.text: Site of Arnold's 1891 window-glass works, one of the largest in the U.S. Innovations there included the Lubbers cylinder-drawing machine. It is documented by HAER.
landmarks.address: North of Drey (Nineteenth) Street, west of Constitution Boulevard, Arnold

landmarks.name: Knead Community Cafe
landmarks.text: Western Pennsylvania's first pay-what-you-can community cafe, opened in 2017.

landmarks.name: Fort Crawford site
landmarks.text: Site of a 1777 Revolutionary War stockade at the mouth of Pucketa Creek. Excavations have turned up arrowheads.

landmarks.name: George D. Stuart (Tarentum) Bridge
landmarks.text: A 1,784-foot continuous-cantilever Pratt deck truss bridge carrying PA 366 across the Allegheny River. It opened in 1952.

landmarks.name: C. L. Schmitt (New Kensington) Bridge
landmarks.text: A 1927 truss bridge linking New Kensington with East Deer and PA 28.

landmarks.name: K-9 Officer Derek Kotecki Memorial Park
landmarks.text: A Lower Burrell park that hosts the city's Community Day.

events.name: Festa Italiana
events.when: First weekend of August (Friday evening and Saturday)
events.where: Mount St. Peter Church, 100 Freeport Road, New Kensington
events.text: A volunteer-run Italian festival, held for more than 40 years, with thousands of homemade meatballs, lasagna, pizza and polenta, plus dancing, bingo and children's games.

events.name: Fridays on Fifth

events.text: A food-truck and live-music night presented by the New Kensington Recreation Commission since 2021. The 2026 dates were April 24, May 22, June 26, July 24, Aug. 28, Sept. 25 and Oct. 23.

events.name: City of New Kensington Christmas Parade
events.when: Early December, Saturday at 11 a.m. (December 6 in 2025)
events.where: Fourth and Fifth avenues, downtown New Kensington
events.text: The yearly holiday parade with floats and local marching bands.

events.name: Downtown tree lighting and Mayor's Annual Holiday Dinner
events.where: Downtown New Kensington; New Kensington Fire Department
events.text: A downtown tree lighting followed by the mayor's community holiday dinner at the fire department.

events.name: Lower Burrell St. Patrick's Day Parade
events.when: Mid-March (the weekend before St. Patrick's Day), 11 a.m.
events.where: Leechburg Road, from Stewart Elementary School to Hillcrest Plaza, Lower Burrell
events.text: Started during the COVID-19 lockdown, the parade has grown to more than 40 participating groups.

events.name: Lower Burrell Community Day
events.where: K-9 Officer Derek Kotecki Memorial Park, Lower Burrell
events.text: A day of food trucks, live entertainment and 45+ vendors that benefits Lower Burrell city parks. Organizers hope to make it a yearly event.

events.name: Arts, Beats and Treats
events.where: AK Research Park (former Alcoa research center), Freeport Road, New Kensington
events.text: A summer festival at the rejuvenated Alcoa property, staged by owner Steve Kubrick. One edition featured a display of Alcoa Kensington Ware.

events.name: Skyy Moore Summer Jam
events.text: A yearly community event for local kids hosted by NFL receiver and New Kensington native Skyy Moore.
